name: Tiwanaku
summary: A highland Andean civilisation beside Lake Titicaca, known for megalithic stonework such as the Gate of the Sun and for raised-field farming.

knownFor.label: Gate of the Sun
knownFor.note: A carved stone gateway with a central staff-god figure.

knownFor.label: Raised-field farming
knownFor.note: Raised beds with water channels that protected crops from frost.

location.value: Western Bolivia, near Lake Titicaca, about 70 km from La Paz.

terrain.value: The Altiplano, a high plateau about 3,800 m above sea level.

climate.value: A long drought from about 1000 CE is often linked to its collapse.

resources.value: Llama and alpaca herds, potatoes, quinoa, and lake fish.

disasters.value: A long drought from about 1000 CE damaged farming.

population.value: About 10,000–20,000 people at the site around 800 CE (a conservative estimate).

urbanisation.value: Surface remains cover about 4 km², with temples, platforms and houses.
urbanisation.source: Wikipedia: Tiwanaku (checked 6 Nov 2026); Janusek, Ancient Tiwanaku (2008)

migration.value: Colonies were set up in lower valleys (such as Moquegua).

economicBase.value: Raised-field farming (suka kollus), herding, and llama caravans.

tradeRoutes.value: Llama caravans linked the lake region with the coast and the forest.

wealth.value: No estimate is possible for this period.

moneyAndTax.value: No coinage. Labour obligations were probably owed instead.

inequality.value: Elite and religious leaders lived in the central city.

governmentType.value: Probably a state led by a religious and political elite.

keyRulers.value: No rulers are known by name; there was no writing.

institutions.value: Little is known; large temples suggest strong religious leadership.

stability.value: Long-lived: about 500–1000 CE at its height.

armyAndTech.value: Little evidence of warfare; influence spread through trade and religion.

territoryChange.value: Influence spread around Lake Titicaca and to the coast.

alliancesRivals.value: Both rival and partner of the Wari state to the north-west.

inventions.value: Raised-field farming that protected crops from frost.

scienceEducation.value: No written language; skill in raised-field farming and stone working.
scienceEducation.source: Wikipedia: Tiwanaku (checked 6 Nov 2026); Janusek, Ancient Tiwanaku (2008)

openness.value: Unknown; it had colonies and trade links with distant valleys.

religion.value: Worship of a staff god, possibly an early form of Viracocha.

languageWriting.value: No written language. Puquina is proposed as its language.

artsArchitecture.value: Decorated ceramics, monumental structures and megalithic blocks.

socialStructure.value: An elite, priests, craftspeople, farmers and llama herders.

sharedIdentity.value: A shared religious centre near Lake Titicaca.

neighbours.value: The Wari state to the north, a rival and partner.

ideasReligions.value: Its religious imagery influenced later Andean peoples, including the Inca.

colonisation.value: Set up colonies in other ecological zones (e.g. Moquegua).

riseSignals.value: From about 500 CE it grew into a major ceremonial and political centre.

peakPeriod.value: About 800 CE, with 10,000–20,000 people at the main site.

declineSignals.value: Drought that ruined the raised-field farming system.

outcome.source: Wikipedia: Tiwanaku (checked 6 Nov 2026); Janusek, Ancient Tiwanaku (2008)

overallCertainty.value: Low to medium; no written records. Second source: Wikidata gives 400–900 CE; Wikipedia gives c. 110–1050 CE.

notes: People living at the main site only.
